Scaffold up, roof stripped back to the purlins.

Five frames, one room.

A blank exterior wall became a covered garden room with a built-in braai and a wall of bifold doors onto the pool. No structure existed here nine weeks earlier — just brick, a flat patch of lawn, and a client who wanted to stop carrying plates outside in the rain.

The frame above cycles through the build in the order it actually happened: framing, insulation, the finished braai from two sides, and the doors that tie it all together. Read the full account, movement by movement, in the Journal.

Field note

Why plaster needs two weeks you can't see

Look closely at the grey wall in most of our site photos and you'll notice it isn't painted — it's a scratch or float coat, cement and sand troweled on over brick or block and left to cure. Plaster doesn't dry so much as it slowly gives up water as it hardens, and rushing that process is the single most common cause of hairline cracking and blown paint we get called back to fix on other people's work.

On a Cape Town job, we budget roughly a week per coat before the next trade touches the wall — longer in damp weather, less in a hot northerly wind. It's the part of a renovation that looks like nothing is happening. It's also the part that decides whether the paint job still looks right in five years.

Journal

Site notes, published as taken

Every job we run gets photographed the way a site inspector would look at it — plainly, and often, at every stage. What follows are two of those records in full: the awkward middle weeks included. Nothing here was staged for the camera; most of it was taken on a phone, mid-task, by whoever had a free hand.

Extension & outdoor room Cape Town ~9 week programme

The Extension That Faces the Pool

A closed brick wall becomes a covered room with a built-in braai, engineered to open completely on a good day.

Before

There was no room here to begin with — just an outside wall, a slab of lawn, and a family who wanted somewhere covered to put a braai without carrying plates through the kitchen every time it rained. The brief was simple to say and, like most extensions, considerably less simple to build: tie a new structure into an existing roofline without weakening it, keep the junction watertight in a climate that gets both driving winter rain and salt-laden summer wind, and make the new space feel like it was always meant to be there rather than bolted on.

During

This is the stage clients tend to find most alarming and we find most reassuring: the roof is open, the new steel is exposed, and the whole thing looks like it might never come together. It's also when the decisions that matter most get made — how the new roofline sheds water into the old gutter run, where the insulation needs to overlap so there's no cold bridge, and how far the new steel beam has to bear onto the existing wall before an engineer will sign off the connection.

We keep scaffolding boarded and covered during this phase specifically because a half-finished roof is the single most weather-exposed moment of any extension. A week of good progress can be undone by one uncovered downpour.

After

The finished room reads as a single gesture, but it's really three trades finishing in sequence: the built-in braai and its flue, then the porcelain patio tiles laid with a fall so water runs clear of the house, then paint and pointing last, once everything below it had a chance to move and settle.

The stainless insert was chosen over an open fireplace specifically because it seals — no smoke drifting back into the new bifold doors twelve feet away, whichever way the Cape Town southeaster happens to be blowing that evening.

From the inside, the same braai reads as part of the room rather than a garden feature — black skirting to match the new joinery, and a sightline straight through to the pool through eight panels of folding glass.

Once the doors are pushed back, there's no threshold left to speak of: the covered room, the patio, and the pool deck become one uninterrupted space, which was the entire point of building it in the first place.

Getting a folding door of this size to sit flush and run smoothly years from now comes down to what's underneath it, not the door itself: a level, waterproofed threshold detail that was set out and checked before a single pane went in, back when this was still an open steel frame under plastic sheeting.

Full refurbishment Cape Town Structural strip-out

Undressing a Cape Cottage

Behind tired paint and eighty years of patch repairs, a small Cape Town cottage is stripped back to brick, replastered, and made ready for its second life.

Before

From the street the cottage still reads as charming — the kind of low white gable and corrugated roof people photograph. Get close to the eaves, though, and the charm gets complicated: cracked bargeboards, timber that's absorbed one too many wet winters, and a roofline that's been patched rather than properly re-fixed more than once. A survey like this always starts outside, because what the roof and walls have been doing for decades tells you far more about what you'll find inside than the seller's description does.

During

That red cross on the wall isn't shorthand for "probably fine to knock through" — it's a wall an engineer has already looked at and signed off, marked on site so the demolition crew removes exactly what's approved and nothing more. Old Cape cottages were often built as a run of small load-sharing rooms, and it's easy to assume a wall is decorative until you've opened the ceiling and traced what it's actually holding up.

With the ceiling down, you can see the original timber roof structure for the first time in decades — sound in places, badly weathered in others, and the reason this stage of a refurbishment always takes longer to price accurately than a new build does. You're not designing from a blank page; you're responding to whatever the building tells you once it's opened up.

The plywood underfoot in Fig. 04 isn't the finished floor — it's a working deck, screwed down over the joists so trades can move materials and tools around without damaging whatever flooring gets specified later. You'll notice the wall behind it is only half-plastered: that's not an unfinished photo, it's a plasterer working in stages across a long run of wall so no single section dries faster than its neighbour, which is what causes visible joins once it's painted.

After

We're showing you this room honestly rather than dressed for a brochure: the walls are plastered and the openings are square, but the floor is still bare screed, the light fittings are pigtails waiting for their final fix, and there's no furniture in sight. This is what "ready for finishes" actually looks like on site — every wet trade has cleared out, and everything from here is dry work: flooring, paint, cabinetry, and the electrician back for a second and final visit.

It's a less photogenic milestone than a styled reveal, but it's the one that matters most to us: the point where the building has stopped fighting the plan and the plan can finally just get finished.

Services

A field guide, not a price list

"Renovation" covers a lot of very different weeks on site. Here's a plain account of what each of the following actually involves, in roughly the order you'd encounter it on a real job — not a sales list, just what the work is.

New builds

Starting from soil

A new build begins long before the first brick — soil testing, foundation design, and a structural engineer's sign-off, all before we're allowed to break ground. From there it's a strict sequence: foundations, structure, roof, then the services and finishes layered in behind a weathertight shell. We run one site diary and one point of contact from the first excavation to the final snag list, so decisions made in week two don't get forgotten by week thirty.

Renovations & refurbishment

Reading the building first

There's a real difference between a cosmetic refresh and a full refurbishment, and it usually isn't visible until walls come open. A refurbishment means stripping back to what's structurally sound, confirming it with an engineer where load-bearing walls are involved, and rebuilding from there — plumbing and wiring included, not just paint and flooring. We price refurbishments with contingency built in for exactly this reason: old buildings rarely match their drawings.

Extensions

Joining new to old

Every extension has one detail that decides whether it looks built-on or built-in: the junction between new structure and existing wall or roof. That's where waterproofing fails if it's rushed, and where an engineer's beam calculation matters more than the finish choices that come later. We set that junction out and get it inspected before anything above it gets closed in, because it's the one mistake you genuinely cannot fix from the inside afterwards.

Plastering & drywall

Coats, not a coat

Solid plaster goes on in stages — a scratch coat keyed into the brick, a float coat to true up the surface, and a skim coat for the final finish — with drying time between each one. Drywall partitions move faster but still need properly staggered, taped and skimmed joints, or they telegraph through paint within a year. We schedule both around the weather, not just the calendar, because a rushed coat in damp Cape Town air is the most common cause of callbacks in this trade.

Project management

One diary, one person accountable

Every site we run gets a daily photographic record and a single accountable manager — the same discipline behind this journal. It's how we catch a plumbing chase that's slightly out of position before the wall closes over it, and how a client gets a straight answer about programme instead of five different subcontractors' opinions. Variations get written down and priced before they happen, not explained afterwards on the invoice.

Electrical & plumbing coordination

First fix, second fix

Wiring and pipework happen in two visits for a reason: first fix, while walls are open, and second fix, once plastering and tiling are done. The coordination work is making sure every switch, socket, geyser connection and drain is in its final position before that first fix happens — because reopening a finished wall to move a plug point is expensive, and it shows. We walk the electrical and plumbing layout with the client before any chasing starts, not after.

About

Why a construction company keeps a journal

TM Construction and Refurbishment builds and refurbishes homes across Cape Town — new builds, extensions, and the kind of full strip-out refurbishment that turns up more questions than the original brief did. This journal exists because of something we'd do anyway, not instead of it.

The photographs come first

Every site we run gets photographed daily, methodically, by whoever's managing it that day. It isn't done for marketing — it's done so that a wall nobody can see anymore can still be accounted for: where the chase runs, what the insulation looked like before the board went over it, what the engineer actually signed off on site rather than on a drawing. That habit is the only reason a site like this journal can exist at all — the record was already being kept.

Publishing the unfinished parts

Most construction marketing shows the reveal and skips the middle. We think the middle is the part worth trusting — the half-plastered wall, the open roof, the plywood subfloor nobody photographs for a brochure. If you can see how a job was actually run, you don't have to take our word for how it'll go. That's the whole premise of this journal: fewer claims, more site photographs, in the order they were taken.

"We photograph the wall before we plaster it, and after — because the wall in between is the only proof anyone has of what's inside it."

— from the site diary
